turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. ____. Well, honestly, my supervisor kind of told me I needed to get this checked out or I'm gonna be in huge trouble. I work on a production line—I do the quality checks, which means I have this specific station where I'm supposed to stay put for my whole shift, except for my two fifteen-minute breaks. But the thing is... I just keep leaving my station. 

Like, I'll be sitting on my stool watching the belt, and the next thing I know, I'm up and walking across the factory floor to talk to someone on line four, or I'm wandering over to the loading dock. I just take off before I even think about it! My legs just sort of decide we're moving and I'm already halfway down the aisle before I realize I left my spot. 

And it happens during our morning shift meetings, too. We have these huddles where we're all supposed to sit in the breakroom and listen to the daily goals, and I'm constantly popping up out of my chair, pacing around, going to the trash can, sitting back down, getting right back up... I just can't stay glued to the chair. Anyway, my supervisor, Gary, he pulled me aside on Tuesday—or maybe it was Wednesday?—and he said it's becoming a major safety problem. He says with all the forklifts and heavy machinery moving around, I can't just be darting away from my post without looking. I really need this job, you know, since I didn't finish high school, it pays better than anything else I can get right now, but I just don't know how to stop myself from getting up.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly describes repeatedly leaving their work station and popping up out of their chair during meetings when they are expected to remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had this same kind of trouble sitting still or staying in one place since you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh my gosh, yes. It’s honestly been exactly like this for as long as I can remember. Even way back in elementary school, I was always *that* kid. You know, the one who just absolutely could not stay in her seat to save her life. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she actually taped a big square around my desk on the floor with this bright blue painter's tape and told me I couldn't step outside the square during lesson time. But I'd still end up wandering over to the class pet, or I'd just be walking around the back of the room looking at the bulletin boards before I even realized I had stood up. 

And it wasn't just the walking around, either. I was constantly talking over the teachers. Like, they'd be right in the middle of explaining a math problem or reading a book, and a thought would just pop into my head and I'd blurt it right out loud, just completely interrupt the whole class. My mom was always so mad at me because I got notes sent home in my folder practically every single week. It was this yellow take-home folder, and the bad notes from the teacher were always on pink paper. I'd try to hide them under my mattress or shove them at the very bottom of my backpack, but she always found them eventually. And the notes always said the exact same thing: that I was wandering around the room again, or I was blurting things out, or I wouldn't stay seated. 

So, yeah, it’s not a new thing at all. It’s just that back then, the worst that happened was a pink slip and getting grounded by my mom, but now Gary is talking about safety hazards and firing me, and I really, really can't lose this job.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states she could not stay in her seat during elementary school and would wander around the classroom.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient describes how she would frequently blurt thoughts out loud during class.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions constantly talking over teachers and completely interrupting the class.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever gotten into a lot of trouble for things like lying, stealing, fighting, destroying property, or deliberately breaking rules?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I'm not a bad person or anything. I don't go around looking for trouble, you know? Like, I've never stolen anything, not even a candy bar when I was a kid. My mom was super strict about that kind of stuff, especially since it was just the two of us and she worked so hard. If she ever caught me taking something that wasn't mine, oh man, I wouldn't have seen the light of day for a month. 

And fighting? No way. I'm actually really non-confrontational. If people start arguing, I'm usually the first one to try and defuse the situation or just walk away. Like, the other day in the breakroom, these two guys from shipping were getting into it over the microwave, and I just could not handle the tension, so I left and ate my lunch outside on this little concrete bench by the dumpsters. It wasn't the best view, but it was better than being around all that yelling. 

I don't break rules on purpose, either. That's the thing that's so frustrating about the whole situation with Gary and my job. I *want* to follow the rules. I know I'm supposed to stay at my station. I know the safety protocols. We had to watch this whole two-hour video during orientation about forklift safety and staying in the designated pedestrian walkways, and I actually paid attention! I took notes and everything because I really wanted to do a good job. I'm not trying to be defiant or difficult. It's just... my body does it before my brain can catch up and say, "Hey, remember the rules?" It's never malicious, I promise. I just... I don't know, I just can't seem to help it.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to leaving his work station despite knowing he is supposed to stay there, stating his body moves before his brain can stop it.
symptom_reasoning.S077: The patient explicitly denies fighting or being confrontational, stating he avoids arguments and walks away from tension.
